topics.body:
Preserve exact integer mixture allocations after normalizing weights. Floating-point roundoff can turn `1001 / 64000 * 64000` into a value just below 1001; truncation then silently moves one document to the largest component. Snap values within 1e-9 of an integer before the existing remainder allocation.

All 23 mixture tests pass, including the normalized-count regression. The affected suite passed 1,591 tests with seven skips; its five checkpoint-path failures reproduce unchanged on main `671c7bcf78`. Mechanical checks and independent library/advisory reviews passed. Reproduction source: #10789.

comments.body: @weaverbot do wholistic review. Double check this change is safe

On it — https://loom.oa.dev/s/tfmllxjl

- 🟢 `Nov  2 17:40Z` Holistic review complete: no findings. https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10793#issuecomment-6583997990

🤖 Holistic review of `c11221d75bc21c46a092e3404020b307d6e822a0`. No findings.

Before this change, `1001 / 64000 * 64000` evaluates to `1000.9999999999999`; truncation assigned one of the smaller source's examples to the largest source. The new tolerance snaps that expected count to 1001 before the existing truncation and remainder rule. The resulting counts feed block assignments, stage offsets, exhaustion calculations, and `sequence_counts_before_block`, so those paths use the same corrected allocation. The regression checks the complete block against disjoint finite sources and detects both the omitted and repeated example.

Direct execution of the changed allocator with NumPy passed 56 exact integral splits and 10,000 normalized random mixtures; all random allocations were nonnegative and summed to their block size. The correction intentionally changes the data sequence for existing configurations that hit this rounding error, including runs resumed from an old checkpoint. I could not rerun pytest here because this worktree's virtual environment has no test dependencies and package downloads are unavailable; the suite results in the PR body remain author-reported.

This issue tracks switching the hero run ([#8435](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8435)) from 16K to 65K (65,536-token) context. Run status lives in [#8506](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8506); the 16K switch was [#9615](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9615) and [#10101](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10101).

**Plan.** Hand off at **permanent step-372000** of 390,251, which the live run writes near **Mon 11-02 03:00 UTC (Sun 11-01 19:00 PST)**, and launch 65K that night; the fallback is Mon 11-02 ~09:00 PST from the same checkpoint. Run 65K on the 16K mesh, CP1 × EP64, with capacity factor 1.5 and qk_mult 1.66. The critical path is the deploy PR ([#10820](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10820), B1) and its one-rack test (C1).

**Status (11-02 04:03 UTC): GO.** `hero-ctx65k-step372k` launched at 03:25 UTC from `6e6924fedd`, restored step-372000 and passed every F2 gate at step 372,102 on its first attempt: median 16.05 s/step, drop fraction ~3.5e-4, peak HBM 127.8 GiB, loss 0.020 below the parent's over the control window. Projected finish ~Thu 11-05 15:00 UTC. Details: [comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10821#issuecomment-6568749068), [W&B cutover report](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/hero-ctx65k-step372k:-65K-context-cutover-at-step-372,000--VmlldzoxODIzOTYyMw==).

## Timing

On 11-01 we chose step-372000, 0.84T tokens (4.7%) at 65K, over step-366000 (1.12T, finishing Sat 11-07) and a manual checkpoint at Monday's relaunch (0.68T), so the 262K extension can finish this week. #8435 planned the last ~5%; Marin's 67B-A2B trained its last 1T of 10T tokens at 65K. Step, token and LR fractions coincide, since every step has 46,137,344 tokens and LR decays linearly.

| Handoff | Step | Tokens left at 65K | Finish at 65K (UTC) | Finish at 16K (UTC) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mon 11-02 03:00 UTC (tonight) | 372,000 (95.3%) | 0.84T | Thu 11-05 ~17:30 | Thu 11-05 ~03:00 |
| Mon 11-02 17:00 UTC (fallback) | 372,000, discarding ~3,500 16K steps | 0.84T | Fri 11-06 ~07:30 | |

Estimates use the live run's 14.19 s/step since its 10-30 launch, including checkpoint writes, ~16.8 s/step at 65K with the same overhead, and ~1.25 h for the switch.

## Configuration

One GB200 rack, restored from step-300000, 500 steps per arm, same code, run back to back:

| Arm | s/step | Drop fraction | Peak HBM (GiB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [CP4 × EP16, capacity factor 1.15](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-prec65k-cp4-01) | 14.699 | 2.41e-3 | 127.6 |
| [CP1 × EP64, capacity factor 1.5](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/tok350-prec65k-cp1cf15-01) | 15.397 | 9.80e-4 | 128.4 |

- **CP1 × EP64 (decided 10-31).** It is 4.7% slower per step than CP4, about 3 h over the rest of the run. It drops 2.5× fewer assignments, needs no launcher change, and its dropless eval passes on main with 12.3 GiB free per GPU. CP4's eval crashes the next train step on main until [#10709](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10709) merges. CP4 work ([#10618](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10618), #10709) continues for the 262K extension.
- **Capacity factor 1.5,** up from the hero's 1.15. At 1.0, CP1 at 65K drops 1.9% of assignments.
- **qk_mult 1.66,** the 262K formula 1.3 × (0.1·ln(65536/4096) + 1).
- **Throughput (estimate):** ~16.3 s/step on the hero, −15% tok/s against 16K.

1. The production launcher has never run 65K; it always runs the hero on 11 racks, so every 65K measurement, including C1, used the one-rack `launch_diagnostics`, which shares its trainer config but not the context history.

4. Eight hero racks run an old IMEX revision that keeps GPU memory imported from a departed peer, which made the 10-29 retries OOM. They are swept while the hero is stopped (G3).

topics.body:
## Description

The hero switched from 16K to 65K training context at permanent step 372000 (#10820, run `hero-ctx65k-step372k`), raising `qk_mult` from 1.48 to 1.66. This experiment evaluates the single handoff checkpoint at several eval lengths and attention scales. It separates three effects on the eval numbers: the eval length itself, the partial-sequence handling in #10711, and the `qk_mult` change.

Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-gradclip-step356k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-372000` (permanent, written by the 16K run). Every run loads this checkpoint and only evaluates; nothing trains.

Setup for every run:
- one GB200 rack (cw-us-east-08a), production priority;
- dropless evals;
- Paloma and Uncheatable;
- eval lengths 4K, 16K and 65K (`eval_dropless/seq_len_<N>/...` metrics).

| Arm | Partial final sequence | `qk_mult` local layers | `qk_mult` global layers | Flags | Lengths |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | truncated (current main) | 1.48 | 1.48 | `--qk-mult 1.48` | 4K, 16K, 65K |
| B | kept with right padding (#10711) | 1.48 | 1.48 | `--qk-mult 1.48`, #10711 branch | 4K, 16K, 65K |
| C | truncated | 1.66 | 1.66 | `--qk-mult 1.66` (the 65K training value) | 4K, 16K, 65K |
| D | truncated | 1.48 | 1.66 | `--qk-mult 1.48 --qk-mult-long-scale 1.1216` | 4K, 16K, 65K |
| E | truncated | 1.48 | 1.86 | `--qk-mult 1.48 --qk-mult-long-scale 1.2568` | 4K, 16K, 65K |

That makes 15 eval runs, at 3 lengths for each of the 5 arms. `--qk-mult-long-scale` multiplies `qk_mult` on the global full-causal layers only, so 1.48 × 1.1216 = 1.66 and 1.48 × 1.2568 = 1.86. Arms C–E use current main's truncation, so they compare against A.

## Hypothesis or Goal

- A vs B: how much the dropped final partial sequence changes Paloma and Uncheatable at each length. The effect should grow with eval length, since a 65K window drops more text per document.
- A vs C: what raising `qk_mult` to 1.66 does to a checkpoint trained at 1.48, at each length, before any 65K training adapts to it.
- C vs D vs E: whether the gain or loss comes from the global layers alone, and whether a larger global scale (1.86) helps long-context evals without hurting 4K.

For every eval (each Paloma and Uncheatable dataset × eval length), also report how truncation changes the tokens scored. Continuous-text validation concatenates a dataset's documents and splits them into windows of the eval length, so truncation drops the final partial window: up to `seq_len − 1` tokens per dataset, and the whole dataset when it is shorter than one window.

| Dataset | Eval length | Total tokens | Scored, truncated (A) | Scored, padded (B) | Dropped by truncation | % dropped |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- These counts come from the eval caches' token counts and need no GPU. Compute them before the runs, then confirm them against the runs' logged scored-token counts.
- Flag datasets that drop entirely at a given length. At 65K, any dataset shorter than 65,536 tokens scores nothing under truncation and drops out of the macro average. That can move the macro by itself, apart from any model change.
- For the macro metrics, list which datasets each arm's macro actually averages over at each length.

Report Paloma macro loss and BPB, and Uncheatable macro loss, per arm and length, with Δ vs arm A.

- Partial-sequence handling: #10711.

topics.body:
Add a daily canary that runs the hero model and training step from main on one GB200 NVL72 rack, so throughput regressions show up before a hero deploy. It uses `launch_diagnostics` with the hero's defaults, restores the pinned permanent checkpoint `step-372000`, trains 35 updates on the production mixture and runs one dropless eval after the last update. Every run sees the same weights and batches, so a step-time change comes from the code. Settings that only the production launcher applies, such as `gate_router_weight_decay` and `prior_context_phases`, are left out; they do not change step time.

The workflow submits at 11:00 UTC (3 AM PST, 6 AM EST) at `batch` priority, the band of the hero-completions sampler, so neither preempts the other. It waits up to five hours for the training job to start, then for the run, and scores it against the per-metric median of the last five scheduled runs from the same checkpoint. Manual dispatches are named `hero-canary-manual-*` and never enter that baseline. A step-time change beyond 1.5% posts its own Slack message, since the run stays green. If no rack frees up in time, `iris_monitor.py wait` cancels the job under the new `--child-wait-timeout-policy shutdown` and the day is skipped with a notice; a failed run alerts through Slack and Loom. The default policy still fails on timeout, so other canaries are unchanged. A healthy run holds the rack for about 20 minutes.

Scored against Matt's one-rack 65K test (`tok350-deploy65k-c1-01`), the report gives 15.572 s/step, 34.41% MFU and 127.9 GiB peak HBM, matching #10820. Over 30 steady steps the median step time is within about ±0.5%, so the report flags changes beyond 1.5%. That threshold is provisional until two same-commit runs measure run-to-run variance.

Over the last two months the GB200 fleet had a median of 8 idle nodes. A five-hour window from 11:00 UTC contained a 30-minute stretch with 16 or more idle nodes on 22 of 62 days, so most days will be skipped until the queue behavior is known from real runs. One rack does not exercise cross-rack collectives or checkpoint recovery. The Loom triage binding needs a `pulumi up` of `infra/loom` after merge, and the first run can only start once the workflow is on main.

The MFU tracker lane is Open-Athena/mfu-tracker#15.

This adds a daily GB200 canary. Each run restores a pinned hero checkpoint on one rack, trains 35 updates and runs one dropless eval. Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

## 6. Code (at run commit [`12d8b6f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be))

**Model** ([`model.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py)) — [`GrugModelConfig`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L160)
- All-MoE routed FFN: [`MoEMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L907) · shared experts [`DenseMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L637)
- QB routing (histogram estimator): threshold/beta [`_qb_beta_hist`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L874), histogram build [`_histogram_from_expert_counts`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L820), applied next-step as stop-grad bias
- Sigmoid combine + renorm-to-2.5: [`_ROUTING_RENORM_SUM`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L58), [combine](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L980)
- LatentMoE + learnable latent RMSNorm: [`latent_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1046)
- RMSNorm on embeddings/readout: [`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223), [`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1203); [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594)
- GatedNorm: [`GatedNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L612)
- XSA (exclusive self-attention): [subtract V-parallel component](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L573)
- Attention head gate (zero-init): [`attn_gate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L583)
- RMS qk-norm: [`rms_norm(q)`,`rms_norm(k)`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L534)
- Partial (half) RoPE, fused: [`_rope`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L553), [`rope_fused`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L541); rope-free global layers via per-layer bounds [L1252](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1252)
- ShortConv: [`ShortConv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L420) → fused Pallas [`short_conv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L52)

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens.

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b).

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

1. Tensorstore restore parallelism bounded by a fixed budget
2. Checkpoint offload cache to 16GB
3. malloc_trim() calls after each checkpoint

in theory 2 will make checkpoints faster (fully async), and 3 will prevent the host OOM recurrence

`malloc_trim` was still inconsistently resulting in OOMs during checkpointing. Restarting on main with the jemalloc changes in.

topics.body:
The ragged all-to-all EP backend hangs at the d6144 hero scale (11 racks, 704 GPUs) within the first hundred steps, on both attempts of the 2026-09-02 deployment. The train step never completes on one rack, the other ten spin in the next AllReduce, and levanter's progress watchdog kills the gang 15 minutes later (`No progress after train_step_started for 909.8 seconds (timeout 900.0); terminating with exit code 124`). No rank logs an error: nothing from NCCL, XLA, CUDA (no Xid), the allocator, or Kubernetes. The hero was rolled back to `04751985c7` (pooled-wave backend), which resumed cleanly from the same checkpoint.

Deployment: main `8e48cdb3ca`, run `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k` resuming `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` from its `step-54000` permanent checkpoint (#8868), `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`, jax 0.11.1, NCCL 2.30.7. Coordinator `/marin/hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k-coord-aade2815`; both attempts ran on the same 176 nodes.

- Attempt 0: steps 54001–54070 completed normally (loss tracks the pooled-wave run step for step at −0.006 nats, drops 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.4%, peak HBM 103.6 GiB). Step 54071 started at 00:23:30Z and never finished; killed 00:38:46Z.
- Attempt 1: restored the same checkpoint, completed step 54000 at 00:45:38Z (loss 1.2364, identical to attempt 0), then hung on step 54001; killed ~01:01Z.

Both hangs are on the first plain train step after a `diagnostic_watch_step` step (54070 → 54071 after seven clean alternations; 54000 → 54001 on the first). The plain and watch steps are two XLA executables that share the NCCL symmetric-memory arena for the ragged all-to-all: each registers its own window at the arena base (`AcquireSymmetricMemory`, `CollectiveMemoryCache`), and equal footprints coexist. #8861 is the same design failing the other way: an executable with a *different* footprint (the capacity-limited eval) makes the next train step fail with `ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument`. Here the footprints are equal and the failure is a silent hang instead of an error, so #8859 (dropless eval only) removes the crash but not this.

Evidence that the hang sits on one rack's EP domain rather than a node fault:

- NCCL RAS (periodic `STATUS` from process 0, `telemetry_v1.levanter`): six minutes into each hang, 64 cross-rack communicators show an AllReduce operation-count skew of exactly 3 (attempt 0: min 10509 / max 10512 at 00:29:43Z; attempt 1: 190 / 193 at 00:52:30Z) and the 704-rank communicator a skew of 2. Before the hangs every communicator was in sync. One member per cross-rack communicator behind by the same count is one whole rack that never entered the step's trailing AllReduces.
- Iris per-task CPU (`iris.task`): exactly 16 of 176 tasks ran at ~4.0 cores while the other 160 ran at ~8.0 during each hang, i.e. one rack in a different wait state from the ranks busy-polling in AllReduce. Attempt 0: tasks 128–143 (zone 129, nodes `s38vxs64 s45sxs64 s51vxs64 s5xvxs64 s69vxs64 s7htxs64 s7qvxs64 s8ktxs64 s8mtxs64 s8yvxs64 s9jvxs64 s9lrxs64 scspxs64 scssxs64 sd8sxs64 shmsxs64`). Attempt 1: tasks 64–79, a different rack on the same node set.
- py-spy thread dumps (`iris process profile threads`) of tasks 0, 83, and 140 during attempt 0: every rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), no Python-side wait; the hang is below XLA's dispatch.
- No node conditions or events on either rack; the cluster's six `HPCVerification=Fail` nodes are elsewhere.

The stall-triggered verbose RAS capture (`trigger = stall`) published nothing in either attempt, so the rank-level view that would name the stuck ranks and the pending collective is missing; the periodic sample is all we have. Neither a 200-step 1-rack smoke restoring the same checkpoint (20 watch/plain alternations) nor the 11,420-step d768 rung reproduced it, so the failure needs more than one rack, i.e. more than one EP domain sharing the job.

Side observations from the same deployment: a cold compile at this shape took 22.9 min for the watch executable plus 6.6 min for the plain one; the data loader's second 64-item prefetch took 920 s (overlapped by compile) where the pooled-wave hero's restarts took under 100 s.

Done when: the ragged backend runs at 11 racks through at least several hundred steps with watch steps enabled without a hang, or the hang is reproduced at smaller multi-rack scale with a GPU-side stack (CUDA core dump / `cuda-gdb` on a stuck rank) that names the kernel or collective.

Related: #8861 (symmetric-window overlap between executables), #8859, #8868, #8506 (hero status log). Side-by-side trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA==

🤖 The mechanism this issue describes is not what the hung run did, and the root cause is still open. Recording what has been ruled out so the next attempt does not repeat it.

The hero had one train executable, not two alternating ones. `launch_scaling_ladder.py:216` sets `WatchMode.INLINE` at the deployed commit `8e48cdb3ca`, so `_make_diagnostic_watch_step` is never built (`train.py:906`), `jit_train_step` computes watch stats on every step, and `step % 10 == 0` only decides whether the host logs them. Step 54071 was byte-identical to 54070 at the XLA and NCCL level. The working pooled-wave hero carries the identical watch config and does not hang.

The capacity-limited evaluator was already disabled. `c3f51e5250` (#8859) is an ancestor of `8e48cdb3ca`, and the dropless evaluator uses `sonic_cute`, which has no all-to-all and registers no symmetric window.

Window aliasing is present but was not the trigger. Two `jit_train_step` executables per rank each register a window at `0xbf80000000`; the cause is now known and is a step-counter sharding mismatch (details in #8861). What turns that aliasing into the `ncclGroupEnd` error is a third executable with a smaller footprint, and no such executable was running here.

Ruled out with evidence, all on one rack at the hero's shape, data and checkpoint unless noted. GIN: the device kernel logs `lsa_size=64 num_ranks=64 gin=false cta_count=152 num_updates_per_replica=6`, and forcing `lsa_size < num_ranks` produces `Device kernel skipped: lsa_size=32 num_ranks=64 requires GIN` followed by a hard `RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed`, so `SupportsGin()` is false in this configuration. That also proves every hero EP domain was a single NVLink domain, since a domain spanning two would have failed loudly rather than stalled. CTA co-residency: the LSA barrier is per-slot, not grid-cooperative — `blockIdx.x` selects a barrier slot and CTA k rendezvouses only with CTA k on its peers — and at `__launch_bounds__(128, 8)` the 152-CTA grid uses a fraction of the device, so `0de14631ea` did not regress residency and the comment in that patch claiming the whole grid must be resident is wrong. `core_count` divergence: every rank reports `cta_count=152`. Hardware: the task-index-to-node map is identical across both attempts and the two stuck 16-task slices share no node. Allocator address churn: `Buffer allocations changed address between module jit_train_step executions` fires only for `parameter` and `live-out` entries, never `temp`, so the arena backing the window is stable. Ragged metadata: `CheckRaggedAllToAllBounds` passed 160 of 160 checks on the same HLO operands the device kernel consumes. NCCL 2.31.2: tested, identical failure (see #8861).

One rack does not reproduce it. Attempts covered two 32-GPU EP domains in one rack (161 steps, clean), raised collective overlap (dies of NaN at step 2, which is #8317's corruption and a different regime), NCCL channel contention, forcing the GIN branch, and a full-fidelity control at 48 layers with mixture data restored from the same `step-54000` checkpoint. The remaining differences at eleven racks — cross-rack collectives sharing the GPUs, and a 704-rank communicator — cannot be built inside one NVLink domain.

What survives is a stall in the LSA barrier that cannot report itself. XLA calls `ncclLsaBarrierSession::sync` in the no-timeout form, and NCCL sets `abortFlag` only `if (isInternal)` (`src/dev_runtime.cc:1175`), so a user-created devComm has none and no watchdog, abort or CUDA error can fire. The barrier epoch is an absolute counter that persists across launches and is zeroed once at `ncclDevCommCreate`, so any divergence is permanent.

Three instrumentation gaps made both attempts undiagnosable, and should be fixed before the next one. The stall diagnostic is never wired: `train.py:968` calls `progress_watchdog.create(process_index=...)` with no `diagnostic=`, so `diagnostic_timeout` stays unset and the stall capture publishes nothing. If it were wired it would run on the wrong process, because `ProgressWatchdogConfig.create` returns `None` for the entire watchdog when `diagnostic_timeout` is set and `process_index != 0`. And the watchdog's `startup_grace_period` defaulted to one hour, which covered attempt 1's entire hang — that run was killed by hand, not by the watchdog.

For the next eleven-rack attempt: set `TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=0` alongside `TF_CPP_VMODULE=ragged_all_to_all_thunk=3,nccl_symmetric_memory=3,gpu_executable=5`, and `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` with `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG,INIT,COLL`. `TF_CPP_VMODULE` alone emits nothing, and `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` emits nothing for this failure class. A diagnostic PJRT build on `marin-community/xla` branch `mcwitt/8870-barrier-timeout` bounds both LSA barrier waits with NCCL's timeout overloads and records the stalled rank, barrier slot and phase, so the next occurrence names itself instead of producing fifteen minutes of silence. It also builds the device kernels against the NCCL the runtime loads: `tensorflow.bazelrc` pins `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION=2.29.7` while the runtime installs 2.30.7, and the timeout API exists only in the newer headers.

The replay ran through that step and kept going. Since the loss agrees to seven significant figures, the batch, the routing, the optimizer state and the arithmetic there are identical to the run that died. Combined with attempt 1 hanging at 54001 from the same restored state, the trigger is timing, not state, and the failure cannot be forced by choosing a checkpoint or a step.

**On the statistics, stated carefully.** Hero exposure was 75 step-attempts with two hangs; the reproduction ran 235 clean. A one-sided test gives p ≈ 0.06 — suggestive that something differs between the two setups, but not significant. Job-steps are the right unit here, not rack-steps: the hang is a job-level event, so counting all 11 racks as independent trials overstates the evidence.

**Candidates eliminated since the last update.** Concurrent checkpoint I/O: `grep "Saving checkpoint"` across every task log in both attempts returns zero hits, so neither attempt ever wrote a checkpoint. Online W&B: per-step tracker cost was 3.73-3.84 ms at every detail step and the wandb thread was idle in `selectors.select` at the py-spy dump. The NCCL RAS probe: it ran in both attempts at a 600 s cadence taking 69-83 ms, and the 00:29:43.8Z poll *succeeded during the hang*, so process 0 and NCCL's in-process listener were responsive while the gang was wedged. A rank silently falling off the device-kernel path: `RaggedAllToAllThunk::RunCollective` returns `InvalidArgument("RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed")` when `xla_gpu_allow_ragged_all_to_all_nccl_send_recv_fallback` is false, which is the deployed setting, so such a rank fails loudly rather than desynchronising quietly, and no attempt logged an error. Two ragged kernels sharing barrier slots: the hero forces `--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit=1`, so collectives cannot be co-resident.

**The version skew, which is a real defect on its own.** `tensorflow.bazelrc:192` pins `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION="2.29.7"` while the runtime resolves to 2.30.7. NCCL's `ncclDevCommCompat_v22907` shim then forces `ginType = NONE` and gates `deviceApiSupport` on `ncclTeamLsa(comm).nRanks == comm->nRanks`. That explains structurally why `SupportsGin()` is false — it was never a configuration choice — and why the device kernel only ever runs on the per-rack EP64 clique, so eleven racks are eleven independent barrier domains whose hazard adds with rack count while nothing couples them. It also means the deployed kernel is compiled without 2.30's bounded `sync(..., timeoutCycles)` overload and without its system-scope release fence in `arrive`, which is exactly why the stall cannot report itself.

**Leading remaining hypothesis.** A stray peer store from the copy loop landing inside the devComm resource window and corrupting the barrier state. Every symmetric window, including the one holding the barrier epochs, lives in the same `devr` VA reservation with a common `stride4G`, and the barrier epoch is an absolute per-slot counter that is never reset or exchanged, so any divergence is permanent: a peer that falls behind makes its partner spin on a comparison that wraps to ~2^32, with `abortFlag == nullptr` for user devComms and no timeout. One sub-case has a matching upstream fix we do not carry: NCCL `0d7243b`, "Mitigate loadConst `__ldg` regression", replaces the non-coherent `__ldg` read of `lsaFlatBase`/`stride4G` with a plain dereference, and those window pointers are rewritten at run time by `ncclDevrReplaceSegmentWindowsIfNeeded`.

**Instrumentation now exists, and did not before.** `CUDA_` was missing from the dispatcher's forwarded env prefixes, so the GPU core-dump variables could never reach a training gang; with that fixed the driver creates one dump pipe per rank. A dump must be taken with `CUDA_COREDUMP_GENERATION_FLAGS=skip_abort,skip_global_memory,skip_constbank_memory`: the default writes 62 GB and SIGABRTs the process, which killed all 64 ranks of a smoke gang and lost the dump with the pod, while the flags give 283 MB. Even so it is terminal within about two minutes (measured at 2:36 and 1:55), so it must trigger, read and upload in one round trip and go last. A dump taken mid-kernel names the resident kernel and gives a per-block state table, which matters because the LSA barrier is per-slot indexed by `blockIdx.x` and that table therefore names the diverged slots directly. NCCL RAS `VERBOSE STATUS` can also be triggered by hand during a hang, answering in ~4 ms with the per-collective min/max that showed the AllReduce skew of exactly 3. Do not attach `cuda-gdb` to a live process: an attach to PID 1 returned nothing in 150 s and took the gang down.

**Next.** A wheel built with the device kernels compiled against the run-time NCCL 2.30.7 exists as `marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-ca0716a2da95`; it removes the skew, adds bounded LSA barriers that record rank, slot and phase, extends the bounds check to the device path, and promotes the transport line to INFO. 🤖 Follow-up with the experimental record from the overnight session. Four more mechanisms eliminated, three of them by direct experiment rather than inference, and two of them hypotheses raised in this issue's earlier comments. Root cause still not determined; what follows is what a next attempt should not spend time on.

**Residency starvation is refuted.** The concern that the ragged kernel's grid cannot stay fully resident is real in principle — the LSA barrier makes CTA k wait on CTA k of every peer, and a CTA that is never scheduled stalls its peers forever, while the already-resident CTAs spin holding their SMs and never yield, so nothing can free what the missing CTAs need. The pre-patch wheel `marin-xla-pjrt-20260828-c9526e8c0272` is maximally exposed to this: it sizes the grid as `kGridSmMultiplier * core_count` where `kGridSmMultiplier = kRaggedAllToAllDeviceKernelCtasPerSm = 8`, i.e. 1216 CTAs against exactly 1216 CTA slots at `__launch_bounds__(128, 8)`. Zero headroom, and its own comment states the requirement. Run at hero shape on one rack it completed **176 steps, roughly 8,400 ragged launches each needing all 1216 CTAs resident simultaneously, with no stall**. Foreign occupancy during the ragged kernel is therefore effectively zero and starvation at the shipped wheel's 8x margin is implausible.

Incidentally, that wheel is about 11% faster: 16.4 s/it and 23.8% MFU against the shipped 18.3 s/it and 21.5%. The grid patch buys a margin this result suggests is not needed, which is worth revisiting on its own merits.

**The autotune-cache race is not this.** The shared node-local `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune` race (#8896) is real and caused a hero retry, but it cannot reach the train step: a 40-step run at a never-compiled shape wrote **zero** autotune results, because this model's heavy GEMMs are Marin's own CUTLASS kernels rather than XLA-autotuned fusions. Autotuning fires only for incidental ops such as the checkpoint slice, so divergent results there cannot change the train step's fusion selection, buffer assignment, arena size or window registration.

**Cross-rack GDR cannot corrupt the barrier.** `devr->lsaFlatBase` is a dedicated `cuMemAddressReserve`; NCCL's network buffers are separate `ncclCudaCalloc` allocations registered through `ncclNetRegMr`. A NIC can only write inside a registered memory region, and a write outside it is rejected by hardware with a completion error rather than landing silently elsewhere.

**Divergent devComm Requirements would be the cleanest mechanism, and both routes to it are closed.** Two ranks requesting different `Requirements` get different devComms, hence different barrier buffers, and since devComm creation is collective each would wait in a barrier the other never joins — silent and permanent, needing no epoch divergence at all. But divergent `lsa_size` takes the `has_remote_peers && !SupportsGin()` branch and fails loudly with `InvalidArgument("RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed")`, and no hero rank logged an error; while divergent `core_count` would be a static per-node property, and the failure moved between two node sets the forensics established are disjoint.

**The kernel's copy loops are bounded.** Both the LSA loop and the inner copy terminate on `num_lsa_updates` and `hi` respectively, `hi` is clamped to each update's own extent, and the GIN branch is dead in this build. Combined with the eliminations above, the barrier is the only place this can hang — that part is now established by construction rather than inference.

**Reproduction attempts, all null:** eleven racks at hero shape (235 steps); maximum executable churn with four executables cycling (~300 steps); registration determinism (all 64 ranks byte-identical, 29 registrations, same order and offsets); cold autotune at a novel shape; zero-headroom residency (176 steps); four EP cliques on one rack (189 steps); and a second transfer geometry at `--latent-dim 2048 --capacity-factor 1.37`, which changes stride and alignment in every offset the copy computes (192 steps).

A single rack cannot reach the remaining space, and the reason is structural: symmetric windows are registered only by the ragged path (`--xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`), so extra communicators and expert-domain splitting do not emulate eleven racks. Closing this needs the failure state observed. The capture path is now armed by default on the ragged transport, so the next occurrence should name itself rather than produce fifteen minutes of silence.

🤖 The hung run pinned a QuACK version with a concrete matrix-multiplication (GEMM) scheduler defect. This is a new lead; the cause of #8870 remains unproved.

The deployed commit `8e48cdb3ca` [pins QuACK 0.6.1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e48cdb3ca/lib/levanter/pyproject.toml#L96), and the archived attempt-0 task-1 setup log confirms `quack-kernels==0.6.1`. The ragged backend's [activation GEMMs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e48cdb3ca/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/sonic_cute.py#L57) use Cluster Launch Control (CLC), which lets resident GPU thread blocks take over work from pending clusters, with variable-length expert groups. The audited package source matches the [0.6.1 release](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/02c7f69881737731173a6a009aeb6f032e449b61/quack/tile_scheduler.py#L504).

That scheduler can observe a failed CLC cancellation, leave its work loop, and then issue more cancellations through its unconditional `cancel_pending_tail` path. NVIDIA's [PTX specification](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.0.0/parallel-thread-execution/index.html#parallel-synchronization-and-communication-instructions-clusterlaunchcontrol-try-cancel) defines further cancellation requests after a GPU thread block observes failure as undefined behavior. The drain also issues asynchronous requests without waiting for their responses before exit.

Upstream [58cb592a1a6e](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/commit/58cb592a1a6e) replaces this path with a conditional, response-checked drain and a separate response buffer. Its [investigation](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/58cb592a1a6e/AI/clc_spurious_invalid_investigation.md) reports stale GEMM output tiles with a second process sharing the GPU and multiple queued GEMM launches, plus a separate GPU-error hazard from requests still in flight at block exit. Those experiments used B300; they do not establish the behavior of our GB200 run. The specification violation does not prove it caused our silent hang, and the cached GPU binary from the original run has not yet been checked against that source.

If this defect prevents a rank's GEMM from completing, the other ranks in its expert-parallel group could wait indefinitely at the next ragged barrier. The [earlier bounded-copy-loop argument](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5537281960) does not exclude a preceding kernel that never completes. Next is a comparison of the original scheduler and a narrow drain fix under finite competing GPU work, checking for incorrect outputs, timeouts and GPU errors at the production matrix dimensions. Each version will use a separate compilation cache so the treatment executes newly compiled code.

This is the strongest evidence so far that #8870's root cause is a fabric fault on specific NVL72 domains rather than anything in the ragged kernel, which merely fails silently where NCCL's host path eventually fails loudly.

**Timeline (2026-09-05, UTC), `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k` on the same 176 nodes and the same rack map as both 09-02 hang attempts and the 09-04 window.** Last step 65069 completed at 17:19:31. Nothing was logged by any rank for the next fifteen minutes; Iris's py-spy dumps at 17:21 and 17:31 show every sampled rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), i.e. blocked on the device — the #8870 shape exactly. At **17:34:36.549 task 162 rank 1 on `s2grxs64` (rack 10, NVLink domain `dh1-r137`)** logged the first `CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED: Invalid access of peer GPU memory over nvlink or a hardware error` (from `cudaFreeAsync`, `gpu_cudamallocasync_allocator.cc:414`); the other rack-10 nodes followed within 0.5 s, racks 2 and 6 by 17:34:37.8, and every rack by 17:34:43 — 88 of 176 tasks logged the fault, the rest were taken down by fate sharing. Iris restarted the gang; it resumed from the hourly temp `step-64944` at 17:38, so the event cost 125 steps plus 20 minutes. It is healthy again (step 65623 at 20 s/step).

**Why this bears on the ragged hangs.** The pooled-wave transport moves data through NCCL's host-driven path, where a fabric fault eventually surfaces as a contained CUDA error and the driver tears the context down. The ragged device kernel spins in an LSA barrier with `abortFlag == nullptr` and, on the wheel that hung, no bounded wait, so the same fault produces fifteen minutes of silence followed by the 900 s progress watchdog — which is what both 09-02 attempts looked like. The fifteen-minute latency before the contained error is itself notable: the fault was in progress, invisible, for as long as the ragged hangs lasted before the watchdog fired.

**The three racks now line up with three independent fabric observations.** Rack 10 (`dh1-r137`): today's fault origin; and `s2grxs64` is the node that supplied the 22:40:30 straggler in the window (task 162, 124 ms). Rack 8 (`dh1-r129`): the 09-02 attempt-0 stall node set; a 5.009 s NVLS multicast bind at window startup (9-12× every other rack); the only repeat straggler node; and `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 is a flapping NVLink — 505 recovery events lifetime, +3 in a 21-minute sample last night and +1 more since, read-only from the running hero, the only counter that moved anywhere in a five-rack sweep. Rack 9 (`dh1-r136`): stragglers in the window, no counter evidence yet. Racks 0-7 show none of this. Rack 10's own GPU-side link counters did not move across today's fault, so the error is on the switch side or a non-link hardware error; node `dmesg`/XIDs are not visible from inside the containers.

**What this changes.** The 09-04 deep-dive (`scratch/8870/window/deepdive/`, eleven streams) had already falsified the cross-rack collective-stall mechanism and left "a per-GPU transient of 25-160 ms, ≥11× more frequent on racks 8-10, with nothing upstream of the GPU to blame." A fabric fault that stalls whatever is crossing a link, escalating occasionally to a contained error or a permanent stall, fits every measurement in this issue, including why attempt 0 hung on rack 8 and why one-rack reproductions on healthy racks never reproduced anything. It does not explain attempt 1 (rack 4, `dh1-r124`), which shows nothing in any sweep; that may be a fourth domain or a different event.

**Untested but now less likely as the cause:** the NCCL 2.29.7/2.30.7 compile skew (the ragged wheel that hung compiled its kernels against 2.29.7; every diagnostic wheel since used 2.30.7). It remains the one code difference between the hung configuration and every clean run, and an A/B wheel exists (`marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-355d8f15cc25`), but today's fault happened with no ragged kernel in the picture at all.

**Asks.** (1) Infra: node-level `dmesg`/XID history and fabric-manager/NVSwitch logs for `dh1-r137` around 17:19-17:35 today and `dh1-r129` around 2026-09-04 22:35:04-09; and `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 as a flapping link. (2) Before the next ragged deployment, a pre-flight that reads NVLink error counters and times the first symmetric-window bind per rack, and refuses racks that stand out. (3) The next 11-rack window should run the per-node 1 Hz GPU/NVLink sampler now on the branch (`MARIN_DEBUG_GPU_SAMPLER_SECONDS=1`) with the per-launch barrier reports, so a link recovery and a barrier stall can be joined at one-second resolution.

Data: `scratch/8870/window/hero-20260905-fault-ranks.txt` (first fault per task/rank/node), `gpuhealth{,2,3}/` (three read-only counter sweeps).

🤖 The [QuACK upgrade branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/upgrade-quack-064) includes the [upstream CLC scheduling fix](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/commit/58cb592a1a6ef85a69e37d0b4eb50217b59d20ca). [The follow-up commit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/66c5e81628) adapts the JAX tensor views to QuACK 0.6.4's batch-first calling convention. The original training hang remains unexplained.

🤖 The September 9 production stall adds evidence for a timing-sensitive synchronization failure after a slow data fetch. This is a hypothesis; the blocked GPU operation and root cause remain unknown.

The affected attempt was `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step81k-coord-1515615f`, with 176 tasks and 704 GPU processes. Its setup logs on tasks 94 and 149 report `quack-kernels==0.6.4`, so this recurrence does not support treating the QuACK upgrade as sufficient to prevent hangs. All times below are UTC on September 9.

- Step 81,758 completed at 19:59:39.838 with loss 1.2321685553. No later completed step was retained for this execution.
- At 19:59:50, all 704 processes reported a data fetch taking at least 10 seconds. Subsequently 680 reported at least 20 seconds, 271 at least 30 seconds, and 19 at least 40 seconds. The final warning was at 20:00:20.119. These counts use distinct task/local-rank pairs.
- Retained Python stack captures at 20:09:40–20:09:54 cover all 704 training processes: every main thread was in `train_step` at `moe_hero_ep/train.py:1176`, and every data-prefetch thread was waiting to enqueue into a full queue. This argues against an ongoing data-loader wait as the condition sustaining the stall. Python stacks do not identify the executing GPU kernel.
- NCCL RAS snapshots at 20:07:56 and 20:17:56 show unchanged AllReduce count ranges of 6,238–6,241 across 64 communicators, plus a range of 10,822–10,824 on one communicator. Both snapshots reported all ranks present, with no missing, unresponsive, or considered-dead ranks across 76 communicators; no communicator records were omitted or invalid. Persistent count divergence does not establish that NCCL caused the stall: an earlier GPU operation can prevent a rank from reaching the next collective.

A candidate trigger is unequal rank arrival after the slow fetch exposing a synchronization defect in the ragged collective or another GPU operation. The warnings describe background prefetch, and per-rank fetch-completion and train-step-entry timestamps are missing, so they do not establish that the delayed fetch fed the stalled step. The earlier [NVLink fault evidence](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5554893088) remains relevant; this observation does not exclude hardware or fabric faults.

The discriminating test is a controlled replay with selected ranks delayed before a training step, comparing ragged A2A with the alternative pooled-wave expert-communication backend and capturing per-rank entry times plus verbose RAS and GPU/native stacks if it stalls. That test has not run.

The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/378) preserves the attempt/execution identifiers and Finelog query scope for the retained evidence.

🤖 Audit of the eleven-rack evidence as of September 9, 22:21 UTC: the NCCL 2.30.7 header build is a promising mitigation, but the record does not support treating all four clean windows as tests of that change. My subjective confidence that the header update materially reduces or resolves the specific ragged-A2A hang is about 60%; this is an engineering judgment, not a statistical posterior or a claim that the failure is eliminated.

Installation logs and distinct process-zero `train_loss` steps give this corrected inventory. Counts include the completed step carrying the restored step number; the earlier comments reported slightly smaller counts at their observation cutoffs.

| Eleven-rack run | PJRT build | Compiled NCCL headers | Completed step records | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| September 3, `ra2a-8870-w1-hero11` | `e94a45d2a446` | 2.29.7 | 165: 54000–54164 | No recorded hang |
| September 4, `ra2a-8870-w2-hero11` | `e94a45d2a446` | 2.29.7 | 72: 54000–54071 | No recorded hang |
| September 4, `ra2a-8870-w3-hero11` | `3091aa7302d8` | 2.30.7 | 185: 54000–54184 | No recorded hang; instrumented wheel |
| September 9, production attempt `72aad6e7` | `b183c591142c` | 2.30.7 | 217: 81716–81932 | Still progressing at the cutoff |

All four used NCCL runtime 2.30.7. The verified newer-header exposure is therefore 402 completed steps across two runs; 237 additional clean steps used the old headers. The earlier statement that every clean reproduction used newer headers was incorrect. The [first two windows](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5534213125) also omitted the checkpointer's per-step broadcast. The [third window](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5547757908) restored that broadcast but added bounded barriers, wait instrumentation, initialization waits and post-collective device-to-host copies. Its success cannot isolate the header change.

Today's run is stronger evidence. It has 176 running tasks, 704 GPU processes, PJRT `b183c591142c`, NCCL runtime 2.30.7 and QuACK 0.6.4. The wheel's source change from production's `3a8f3392723e` is the two-line NCCL build-default update in [XLA PR #22](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/pull/22). The live `train.py` hash matches main, and the batch-ready host barrier is absent. The preceding production attempt `1515615f` used PJRT `3a8f3392723e` with NCCL 2.29.7 headers and runtime 2.30.7; it completed 43 steps from the same restored step 81716 before stalling. Today’s wheel omits the September 4 diagnostic barrier timeouts and device-to-host wait-record copies. This is useful evidence against those diagnostic copies or the proposed host barrier being necessary for the current improvement. It is still one uninstrumented success, with build toolchain, allocation and timing differences, rather than a randomized wheel A/B or a tested restart sequence. Old-header clean windows and the [September 5 pooled-wave run’s contained NVLink error](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5554893088) keep alternatives credible; that separate failure shows hardware can also cause a similar stall.

There is also preliminary numerical and performance evidence. Comparing today’s run with `1515615f` over matched steps 81726–81758, loss differed by at most 0.000110 nats, with mean treatment-minus-control +0.0000076. The mean of the reported `throughput_mean_mfu` samples was 21.626% for the new wheel versus 22.110% for the earlier attempt, a decrease of 0.484 percentage points (2.19% relative). These 33 matched steps are observational and do not establish a performance regression or non-regression. Sustained training and restart validation remain open.

For reproducibility, the historical execution IDs are `iris:227df97f1c61d78c`, `iris:8a8e59dcdce56776` and `iris:153389937ce684a7`; today's control and treatment are `iris:a8d3026cb58a0341` and `iris:aa61bafbfdef1160`. Counts use `levanter.metrics`, `name='train_loss'`, `process_index=0`, deduplicated by execution and step. The Marin hub lagged today's regional metrics: 196 records through 22:13:27 UTC on the hub, with the remaining 21 through 22:21:17 UTC verified on `cw-us-east-08a`. The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/378) and [wheel-pin PR #9062](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9062) track the current mitigation.

🤖 The source audit found two concrete deadlocks in the remote GIN branch, but neither explains the measured `gin=false` hero path. Zero-size updates skip completion signals that the receiver still counts. Separately, receiver CTA0 can snapshot a shared signal after another CTA's current-launch sends arrive, then wait for an unreachable count. Both predate [3a8f3392723e](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/commit/3a8f3392723e321d806012c5aab492a73bd194c3); these are independently checked protocol schedules, not GPU reproductions.

No missing local CTA synchronization was found in the executed LSA branch: NCCL already joins CTA threads before release publication, and kernel completion joins the matching peer-copy barriers. That result depends on valid metadata, matching grids, serialized barrier resources and CTA progress. It does not locate the original blocked operation. A preceding GEMM or stalled peer-memory transaction can strand peers at the next ragged barrier; the earlier finite-copy-loop argument does not exclude either.

Fresh Finelog analysis confirms larger checkpoint-adjacent dips. Across 1,567 intervals between successive completed-step timestamps per arm (each labeled by its ending step), ragged had eleven intervals above 1.5× its 17.598-second median, all within checkpoint state step through step+4; pooled-wave had one above 1.5× its 19.610-second median. Watch-boundary concentration remains unconfirmed: stalled steps were 54072, 54001, 81759 and 83308, plus three first-step failures after restore. Same-day old-header attempts hung after 43, 0, 0 and 0 completed steps; the new-header trial ran about 300 steps before cancellation and the release hung after roughly 1,590. This is an apparent improvement in exposure before failure, not a controlled failure-rate estimate.

The upstream review found no change to the device-copy/barrier implementation from fork base `dcf304bc5d` through main `5718ca7411` (September 10, 17:11:56 UTC). [52a0596243](https://github.com/openxla/xla/commit/52a05962435a168467cc9f8443d3f83a14cbe2af), which explicitly prevents a deadlock, only changes one-shot debug bounds checking, outside the selected device path. The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/385) now includes the source audit, assumptions, query scope and discriminating measurements. The next decisive capture is the first blocked GPU operation plus per-rank/CTA barrier epochs and stream dependencies. A non-hanging run cannot identify the initiating blocked operation.
🤖 Capture validation is complete. The procedure and limitations are recorded in [the incident note](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/385).
🤖 Updated incident diagnosis and capture limitations: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/420.
🤖 Updated GPU capture findings and diagnostic procedure: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/431.
